rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The whole person's quality of error is attributed to his forelock, describing a part with the quality of the whole.
rows.anchor: فالخطأ صفة الكل وصف به الناصية عكسه كقوله ﴿ إنا منكم وجلون ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reverse construction assigns to a whole person a state belonging to the heart, since fear and dread reside in the heart.
rows.anchor: والوجل صفة القلب ﴿ ولملئت منهم رعبا ﴾ والرعب إنما يكون في القلب

words: ولأبين لكم بعض الذي تختلفون فيه
rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda takes some in these phrases to mean all.
rows.anchor: والثاني إطلاق لفظ بعض مرادا به الكل ذكره أبو عبيدة وخرج عليه قوله

words: ولأبين لكم بعض الذي تختلفون فيه
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The all-for-some reading is challenged because a prophet is not required to explain every disputed matter, such as the Hour and the Spirit.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأنه لا يجب على النبي بيان كل ما اختلف فيه بدليل الساعة والروح ونحوهما

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thaʿlab reads some literally: the threatened worldly punishment may befall them as one part of the threat, without excluding punishment in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: ( يصبكم هذا العذاب في الدنيا وهو بعض الوعيد من غير نفي عذاب الآخرة ) ذكره ثعلب

rows.speaker: الزركشي
rows.claim: Al-Zarkashi supports the literal partial-threat reading: an entire threat may be left unfulfilled, so its partial fulfillment is unproblematic; 40:77 offers a parallel.
rows.anchor: قال الزوكشي ويحتمل أيضا أن يقال إن الوعيد مما لا يستنكر ترك جميعه فكيف بعضه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A specific noun can stand for a general referent: messenger is singular in the example but means the messengers of the Lord of the worlds.
rows.anchor: الخامس إطلاق إسم الخاص على العام نحو ﴿ إنا رسول رب العالمين ﴾ أي رسله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A general expression can refer specifically to believers: those in the earth whom angels ask forgiveness for are identified as the believers.
rows.anchor: السادس عكسه نحو ﴿ ويستغفرون لمن في الأرض ﴾ أي المؤمنين بدليل قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text names a further figure of speech: using the name of a prerequisite for what necessarily follows from it.
rows.anchor: السابع إطلاق إسم الملزوم على اللازم نحو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reverse figure uses a necessary condition to mean the action it entails: asking whether God can give a table means asking whether He will do so.
rows.anchor: الثامن عكسه نحو ﴿ هل يستطيع ربك أن ينزل علينا مائدة من السماء ﴾ أي هل يفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A result may name its cause: provision and clothing are used for rain, which produces them.
rows.anchor: أي مطرا يتسبب عنه الرزق واللباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the phrase about those who cannot find marriage, marriage means the funds and necessities needed to marry.
rows.anchor: أي مؤنة من مهر ونفقة وما لا بد للمتزوج منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cause may be named for its result: inability to hear means inability to accept and act on what was heard.
rows.anchor: العاشر عكسه نحو ﴿ ما كانوا يستطيعون السمع ﴾ أي القبول والعمل به

rows.speaker: الحذاق من النحاة وأهل البيان
rows.claim: Skilled grammarians and rhetoricians hold that speech has only two kinds, report and composition, with no third category.
rows.anchor: الحذاق من النحاة وغيرهم وأهل البيان قاطبة على انحصار الكلام فيهما وأنه ليس له قسم ثالث

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: One proposed taxonomy has ten kinds: calling, questioning, command, intercession, exclamation, oath, condition, assertion, doubt, and interrogation.
rows.anchor: وادعى قوم أن أقسام الكلام عشرة نداء ومسألة وأمر وتشفع وتعجب وقسم وشرط ووضع وشك واستفهام

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: A nine-kind taxonomy drops interrogation because it is included within questioning.
rows.anchor: وقيل تسعة بإسقاط الاستفهام لدخوله في المسألة

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: An eight-kind taxonomy drops intercession because it is included within questioning.
rows.anchor: وقيل ثمانية بإسقاط التشفع لدخوله فيها

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: A seven-kind taxonomy drops doubt because it belongs to the category of report.
rows.anchor: وقيل سبعة بإسقاط الشك لأنه من قسم الخبر

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash divides speech into six kinds: report, inquiry, command, prohibition, calling, and wishing.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش هي ستة خبر واستخبار ولأمر ونهي ونداء وتمن

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another classification has five kinds: report, command, explicit declaration, request, and calling.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم خمسة خبر وأمر وتصريح وطلب ونداء

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Another classification has four kinds: report, inquiry, request, and calling.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم أربعة خبر واستخبار وطلب ونداء

rows.speaker: كثيرون
rows.claim: Many scholars divide speech into report, request, and composition: report can be judged true or false, while the other two cannot.
rows.anchor: وقال كثيرون ثلاثة خبر وطلب وإنشاء قالوا لأن الكلام إما أن يحتمل التصديق والتكذيب أو لا

rows.speaker: المحققون
rows.claim: The authoritative scholars include request within composition: the request to strike coincides with the word, while the later striking is only its requested object.
rows.anchor: والمحققون على دخول الطلب في الإنشاء

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: Some say report cannot be defined because its nature is difficult to capture.
rows.anchor: وقد اختلف الناس في حد الخبر فقيل لا يحد لعسره

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: Others say report is self-evident because people necessarily distinguish it from composition; the Imam in al-Mahsul prefers this view.
rows.anchor: وقيل لأنه ضروري لأن الإنسان يفرق بين الإنشاء والخبر ضرورة ورجحه الإمام في المحصول

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو بكر والمعتزلة
rows.claim: Al-Qadi Abu Bakr and the Muʿtazilites define report as speech admitting truth or falsehood; against the objection of God's report, al-Qadi says language permits either possibility.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو بكر والمعتزلة الخبر الكلام الذي يدخله الصدق والكذب

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: Another definition calls report speech that admits affirmation or denial, avoiding the objection raised against the prior definition.
rows.anchor: وقيل الذي يدخله التصديق والتكذيب وهو سالم من الإيراد المذكور

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن البصري
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan al-Basri defines report as speech that itself conveys a relation; the definition is challenged because a command also relates an action to its subject.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الحسن البصري كلام يفيد بنفسه نسبة

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: One alternative defines report as speech that itself positively or negatively relates one matter to another.
rows.anchor: وقيل الكلام المفيد بنفسه إضافة أمر من الأمور إلى أمر من الأمور نفيا أو إثباتا

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: Another definition describes report as an utterance explicitly affirming or denying a relation between known things.
rows.anchor: وقيل القول المقتضي بصريحه نسبة معلوم إلى معلوم بالنفي والإثبات

rows.speaker: المتأخرون
rows.claim: Later scholars define composition as speech that brings its meaning into external existence, with report defined by contrast.
rows.anchor: وقال المتأخرين الإنشاء ما يحصل مدلوله في الخارج بالكلام والخبر خلافه

rows.speaker: السخاوي
rows.claim: Al-Sakhawi says Surat Ta-Ha is also called Surat al-Taklim.
rows.anchor: طه تسمى أيضا سورة التكليم ذكره السخاوي في جمال القراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surat al-Shuʿara is also called al-Jamiʿa in Malik's tafsir.
rows.anchor: الشعراء وقع في تفسير الإمام مالك تسميتها بسورة الجامعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surat al-Naml is also called Surat Sulayman.
rows.anchor: النمل تسمى أيضا سورة سليمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surat al-Sajda is also called al-Madajiʿ.
rows.anchor: السجدة تسمى أيضا المضاجع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surat Fatir is also called Surat al-Malaʾika.
rows.anchor: فاطر تسمى سورة الملائكة

rows.speaker: النبي ﷺ
rows.claim: The Prophet called Surat Ya-Sin the heart of the Qur'an; al-Tirmidhi transmits this from Anas.
rows.anchor: يس سماها صلى الله عليه وسلم قلب القرآن أخرجه الترمذي من حديث أنس

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqi transmits a marfuʿ report from Abu Bakr calling Ya-Sin al-Muʿimma, al-Dafiʿa, and al-Qadiya, with promised worldly and next-worldly good, protection from evil, and fulfillment of needs; al-Bayhaqi calls it munkar.
rows.anchor: وأخرج البيهقي من حديث أبي بكر مرفوعا سورة يس تدعى في التوراة المعمة نعم بخيري الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surat al-Zumar is also called Surat al-Ghuraf.
rows.anchor: الزمر تسمى سورة الغرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surat Ghafir is called al-Tawl and al-Muʾmin; the latter title comes from the phrase about a believing man in 40:28.
rows.anchor: غافر تسمى سورة الطول والمؤمن لقوله تعالى فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surat Fussilat is also called al-Sajda and Surat al-Masabih.
rows.anchor: فصلت تسمى السجدة وسورة المصابيح

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Karmani records al-Shariʿa and Surat al-Dahr as names for Surat al-Jathiya.
rows.anchor: الجاثية تسمى الشريعة وسورة الدهر حكاه الكرماني في العجائب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surat Muhammad is also called Surat al-Qital.
rows.anchor: سورة محمد تسمى القتال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surat Qaf is also called Surat al-Basiqat.
rows.anchor: ق تسمى سورة الباسقات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sura beginning Iqtarabat is also called Surat al-Qamar.
rows.anchor: إقتربت تسمى القمر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqi transmits a report from Ibn Abbas calling al-Qamar al-Mubayyida, which whitens its reciter's face on the day faces turn black; al-Bayhaqi grades it munkar.
rows.anchor: وأخرج البيهقي عن ابن عباس أنها تدعى في التوراة المبيضة تبيض وجه صاحبها يوم تسود الوجوه

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqi transmits a marfuʿ report from Ali calling al-Rahman the Bride of the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: الرحمن سميت في حديث عروس القرآن أخرجه البيهقي عن علي مرفوعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Ubayy ibn Kaʿb's codex, Surat al-Mujadila is called al-Zihar.
rows.anchor: المجادلة سميت في مصحف أبي الظهار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: When Saʿid ibn Jubayr called it Surat al-Hashr, Ibn Abbas said to call it Surat Bani al-Nadir instead.
rows.anchor: أخرج البخاري عن سعيد بن جبير قال قلت لابن عباس سورة الحشر قال قل سورة بني النضير

rows.speaker: ابن حجر
rows.claim: Ibn Hajar says Ibn Abbas may have disliked al-Hashr because readers could mistake it for the Day of Judgment, whereas the name here means the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir.
rows.anchor: قال ابن حجر كأنه كره تسميتها بالحشر لئلا يظن أن المراد يوم القيامة وإنما المراد به هنا إخراج بني النضير

rows.speaker: ابن حجر
rows.claim: Ibn Hajar says the common vocalization al-Mumtahana has fatḥa and describes the woman on whose account the sura was revealed; with kasra it describes the sura itself.
rows.anchor: قال ابن حجر المشهور في هذه التسمية أنها بفتح الحاء وقد تكسر فعلى الأول هو صفة المرأة التي نزلت السورة بسببها وعلى الثاني هي صفة السورة

rows.speaker: جمال القراء
rows.claim: Jamal al-Qurra also records al-Imtihan and al-Mawadda as names for Surat al-Mumtahana.
rows.anchor: وفي جمال القراء تسمى أيضا سورة الإمتحان وسورة المودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surat al-Saff is also called Surat al-Hawariyyin.
rows.anchor: الصف تسمى أيضا سورة الحواريين

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Al-Bukhari and others transmit Ibn Masʿud's name for Surat al-Talaq, al-Nisa al-Qusra.
rows.anchor: الطلاق تسمى سورة النساء القصرى كذا سماها ابن مسعود أخرجه البخاري وغيره

rows.speaker: الداودي وابن حجر
rows.claim: Al-Dawudi objects that al-Qusra is not reliably preserved, but Ibn Hajar says this rejects established reports without evidence; qasr and tul are relative, as Zayd ibn Thabit calls al-Aʿraf one of the two longest suras.
rows.anchor: وقد أنكره الداودي فقال لا أرى قوله القصرى محفوظا ولا يقال في سورة من القرآن قصرى ولا صغرى

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Ahmad transmits from Abu Hurayra that the seven revealed forms include the synonymous descriptions knowing, wise, forgiving, and merciful.
rows.anchor: وعند أحمد من حديث أبي هريرة أنزل القرآن على سبعة آحرف عليما حكيما غفورا رحيما

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Ahmad transmits from Umar that Qur'anic variants are all sound unless they turn forgiveness into punishment or punishment into forgiveness; al-Suyuti calls the chains good.
rows.anchor: وعنده أيضا من حديث عمر أن القرآن كله صواب ما لم تجعل مغفرة عذابا أو عذابا مغفرة أسانيدها جياد

rows.speaker: ابن عبد البر
rows.claim: Ibn Abd al-Barr says the seven forms may differ in wording while sharing an understood meaning, with no form contradicting or negating another.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عبد البر إنما أراد بهذا ضرب المثل للحروف التي نزل القرآن عليها إنها معان متفق مفهومها مختلف مسموعها

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb is reported to read 2:20 with alternatives meaning they passed through it or hurried through it, illustrating equivalent wording variants.
rows.anchor: ثم أسند عن أبي بن كعب أنه كان يقرأ

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud is reported to read 57:13 with alternatives meaning give us time or delay us.
rows.anchor: وكان ابن مسعود يقرأ ﴿ للذين آمنوا انظرونا ﴾ أمهلونا أخرونا

rows.speaker: الطحاوي
rows.claim: Al-Tahawi says the seven forms were a concession for people who struggled with one fixed wording because literacy, writing, and precise memorization were difficult; the concession was abrogated when those obstacles passed.
rows.anchor: قال الطحاوي وإنما كان ذلك رخصة لما كان يتعسر على كثير منهم التلاوة بلفظ واحد لعدم علمهم بالكتابة والضبط وإتقان الحفظ ثم نسخ بزوال العذر

rows.speaker: ابن عبد البر والباقلاني وآخرون
rows.claim: Ibn Abd al-Barr, al-Baqillani, and others likewise hold that the seven-form concession ended once its cause was removed.
rows.anchor: وكذا قال ابن عبد البر والباقلاني وآخرون

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: A report through Awn ibn Abd Allah says Ibn Masʿud taught a man who could not pronounce al-athim to recite al-fajir instead, illustrating accommodation in recitation.
rows.anchor: وفي فضائل أبي عبيد من طريق عون بن عبد الله أن ابن مسعود أقرأ رجلا

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد وثعلب والأزهري وآخرون
rows.claim: A tenth view, adopted by Abu Ubayd, Thaʿlab, al-Azhari, and others, understands the seven forms as seven Arabic languages; Ibn Atiyya preferred it and al-Bayhaqi authenticated it in al-Shuʿab.
rows.anchor: القول العاشر إن المراد سبع لغات وإلى هذا ذهب أبو عبيد وثعلب والأزهري وآخرون واختاره ابن عطية وصححه البيهقي في الشعب

rows.speaker: المعترضون
rows.claim: Critics object that Arab dialects number more than seven; proponents answer that the seven means the most eloquent dialects.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأن لغات العرب أكثر من سبعة وأجيب بأن المراد أفصحها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas identifies five of the seven languages with the Hawazin clans Saʿd, Jusham, Nasr, and Thaqif, collectively called the upper Hawazin; Abu Amr says they and lower Tamim were the most eloquent Arabs.
rows.anchor: فجاء عن أبي صالح عن ابن عباس قال نزل القرآن على سبع لغات منها خمس بلغة العجز من هوازن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another route from Ibn Abbas says the Qur'an came in the language of the two Kaʿbs, Quraysh and Khuzaʿa, whose neighboring communities shared a familiar language.
rows.anchor: وأخرج أبو عبيد من وجه آخر عن ابن عباس قال نزل القرآن بلغة الكعبيين كعب قريش وكعب خزاعة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: In a report from al-Shaʿbi, Umar asks a traveling group for the greatest Qur'anic verse and Ibn Masʿud answers the Throne Verse, 2:255.
rows.anchor: أخرج السلفي في المختار من الطيوريات عن الشعبي قال لقي عمر بن الخطاب ركبا في سفر فيهم ابن مسعود فأمر رجلا

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Asked which verse is most wise, Ibn Masʿud answers 16:90, God's command to justice, excellence, and giving to kin.
rows.anchor: قال نادهم أي القرآن أحكم فقال ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud names 99:7–8, the atom's-weight verses, as the most comprehensive verse.
rows.anchor: قال نادهم أي القرآن أجمع فقال

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud identifies 4:123, whoever does evil will be repaid for it, as the saddest verse.
rows.anchor: قال نادهم أي القرآن أحزن فقال

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud calls 39:53, the prohibition on despairing of God's mercy, the most hopeful verse.
rows.anchor: قال نادهم أي القرآن أرجى فقال

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Abd al-Razzaq transmits Ibn Masʿud calling the command to justice the most just verse in the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: وأخرج عبد الرزاق أيضا عن ابن مسعود قال

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Abd al-Razzaq also transmits Ibn Masʿud calling the atom's-weight passage the most wise verse.
rows.anchor: وأخرج عبد الرزاق أيضا عن ابن مسعود قال

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Al-Hakim transmits Ibn Masʿud calling the command to justice the most comprehensive verse for good and evil.
rows.anchor: وأخرج الحاكم عنه قال إن أجمع آية في القرآن للخير والشر

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Al-Tabarani transmits Ibn Masʿud calling 39:53 the verse that gives the greatest hope.
rows.anchor: وأخرج الطبراني عنه قال ما في القرآن آية أعظم فرجا من آية في سورة الغرف

words: ومن يتوكل على الله فهو حسبه
rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Al-Tabarani transmits Ibn Masʿud calling 65:3 the verse that most fully entrusts matters to God.
rows.anchor: وما في القرآن آية أكثر تفويضا من آية في سورة النساء القصرى

words: الله لا إله إلا هو الحي القيوم
rows.speaker: رسول الله ﷺ
rows.claim: Abu Dharr al-Harawi transmits from Yahya ibn Yaʿmar and Ibn Masʿud a Prophetic report naming 2:255 the greatest verse.
rows.anchor: وأخرج أبو ذر الهروي في فضائل القرآن من طريق يحيى بن يعمر عن ابن مسعود قال سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول

rows.speaker: رسول الله ﷺ
rows.claim: The same Prophetic report calls 16:90 the most just verse.
rows.anchor: قال سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول ( إن أعظم آية في القرآن

rows.speaker: رسول الله ﷺ
rows.claim: The same Prophetic report calls the atom's-weight verses the most fear-inducing.
rows.anchor: وأخوف أية في القرآن ﴿ فمن يعمل مثقال ذرة خيرا يره

rows.speaker: رسول الله ﷺ
rows.claim: The same Prophetic report calls 39:53 the most hopeful verse.
rows.anchor: وأرجى آية في القرآن ﴿ قل يا عبادي الذين أسرفوا على أنفسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-najm refers to plants that spread along the ground, while al-shajar grows on a stem.
rows.anchor: ﴿ والنجم والشجر ﴾ النجم ما ينبسط على الأرض والشجر ما ينبت على ساق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-anam means creation.
rows.anchor: 1991 ﴿ للأنام ﴾ الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu al-ʿasf means straw.
rows.anchor: 1992 ﴿ ذو العصف ﴾ التبن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-rayhan means the green part of crops.
rows.anchor: 1993 ﴿ والريحان ﴾ خضرة الزرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase asks about which blessings of God the two addressed beings deny.
rows.anchor: 1994 ﴿ فبأي آلاء ربكما ﴾ بأي نعمة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marij means pure, unmixed fire.
rows.anchor: 1995 ﴿ من مارج ﴾ خالص النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maraja means released or sent forth.
rows.anchor: 1996 ﴿ مرج ﴾ أرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Barzakh means a barrier.
rows.anchor: 1997 ﴿ برزخ ﴾ حاجز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu al-jalal means possessing majesty and greatness.
rows.anchor: 1998 ﴿ ذو الجلال ﴾ ذو العظمة والكبرياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that God will attend to the addressees is a threat; it does not imply that God is occupied with other tasks.
rows.anchor: 1999 ﴿ سنفرغ لكم ﴾ هذا وعيد من الله لعباده وليس بالله شغل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They will not escape God's dominion.
rows.anchor: 2000 ﴿ لا تنفذون ﴾ لا تخرجون من سلطاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuwaz means a flame of fire.
rows.anchor: 2001 ﴿ شواظ ﴾ لهب النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nuhas means the smoke of fire.
rows.anchor: 2002 ﴿ ونحاس ﴾ دخان النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The produce of the two gardens means their fruits.
rows.anchor: 2003 ﴿ وجنى الجنتين ﴾ ثمار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lam yatmithhunna means that none has approached them.
rows.anchor: 2004 ﴿ لم يطمثهن ﴾ يدن منهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naddakhatan means gushing or overflowing.
rows.anchor: 2005 ﴿ نضاختان ﴾ فائضتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Green rafraf refers to seats or couches.
rows.anchor: 2006 ﴿ رفرف خضر ﴾ المجالس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: La taniya means do not weaken in carrying out My command; an anonymous poetic line uses waniytu to attest this sense.
rows.anchor: قال لا تضعفا عن أمري قال وهل تعرف العرب ذلك قال نعم أما سمعت قول الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-qaniʿ is one content with what he receives, while al-muʿtarr goes around to doorways; a poem uses yaʿtarihim for the latter sense.
rows.anchor: قال القانع الذي يقنع بما أعطي والمعتر الذي يعترض الأبواب قال وهل تعرف العرب ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A mushayyad palace is plastered with gypsum; a verse by ʿAdi ibn Zayd attests the verb shadahu for building or coating it.
rows.anchor: قال مشيد بالجص والآخر قال وهل تعرف العرب ذلك قال نعم أما سمعت عدي بن زيد يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuwaz is flame without smoke; a line by Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt attests the word.
rows.anchor: قال الشواظ اللهب الذي لا دخان له قال وهل تعرف العرب ذلك قال نعم أما سمعت قول أمية بن أبي الصلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aflaha means succeeded and prospered; Labid ibn Rabiʿa's line uses the same word as evidence.
rows.anchor: قال فازوا وسعدوا قال وهل تعرف العرب ذلك قال نعم أما سمعت قول لبيد بن ربيعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yuʾayyid means strengthens; Hassan ibn Thabit's line uses ayyadu to attest this meaning.
rows.anchor: قال يقوي قال وهل تعرف العرب ذلك قال نعم أما سمعت قول حسان بن ثابت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nuhas is smoke without flame; the cited anonymous poetic line uses nuhas for this sense.
rows.anchor: قال هو الدخان الذي لا لهب فيه قال وهل تعرف العرب ذلك قال نعم أما سمعت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amshaj means the mingling of the man's and woman's fluids when they meet in the womb; the text begins to cite Abu Dhuʾayb's poetry as evidence.
rows.anchor: قال اختلاط ماء الرجل وماء المرأة إذا وقع في الرحم قال وهل تعرف العرب ذلك قال نعم أما سمعت قول أبي ذؤيب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Muqatil and al-Kalbi report from Ibn Abbas that istawa means settled; al-Suyuti says that, if authentic, it requires reinterpretation because settlement suggests corporeality.
rows.anchor: حكى مقاتل والكلبي عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: Some interpret istawa as istawla, meaning took control.
rows.anchor: ثانيها أن ( استوى ) بمعنى ( استولى ) ورد بوجهين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The istawla interpretation is rejected because God already controls the two realms, Paradise, and Hell, making the Throne's specification pointless.
rows.anchor: أحدهما أن الله تعالى مستول على الكونين والجنة والنار وأهلهما فأي فائدة في تخصيص العرش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The istawla interpretation is also rejected because taking control implies prior opposition and victory, which is unbefitting of God.
rows.anchor: والآخر أن الاستيلاء إنما يكون بعد قهر وغلبة والله سبحانه وتعالى منزه عن ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Asked about istiwa, Ibn al-Aʿrabi says to affirm what God has reported; he rejects istawla because it is said only after overcoming an opponent.
rows.anchor: أخرج اللالكائي في السنة عن ابن الأعرابي أنه سئل عن معنى

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd offers ascended as the meaning of istawa.
rows.anchor: ثالثها أنه بمعنى صعد قاله أبو عبيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ascension interpretation is rejected because God is transcendent above ascending.
rows.anchor: ورد بأنه تعالى منزه عن الصعود أيضا

rows.speaker: إسماعيل الضرير
rows.claim: Ismaʿil al-Darir proposes reading the phrase as al-Rahman rose, with the Throne as what He established.
rows.anchor: حكاه إسماعيل الضرير في تفسيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposal is rejected because it makes ʿala a verb though it is unanimously a preposition; a verb would be written ʿala with alif as in ʿala fi al-ard.
rows.anchor: أحدهما أنه جعل ( على ) فعلا وهي حرف هنا بإتفاق فلو كانت فعلا لكتبت بالألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same proposal requires al-ʿarsh to be nominative, but no canonical reader recites it with that case.
rows.anchor: والآخر أنه رفع ( العرش ) ولم يرفعه أحد من القراء

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: A further reading ends the sentence at on the Throne and begins a new clause, He established what is in the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: أن الكلام تم عند قوله ﴿ الرحمن على العرش ﴾ ثم ابتدأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti rejects the clause break because it disrupts the verse's order and intended meaning, and says it cannot account for the wording in 20:5.
rows.anchor: ورد بأنه يزيل الآية عن نظمها ومرادها

rows.speaker: الفراء والأشعري وجماعة أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ, al-Ashʿari, and other specialists say istawa means turned toward or intended the creation of the Throne; Ismaʿil al-Darir calls this correct, by analogy with 41:11.
rows.anchor: قاله الفراء والأشعري وجماعة أهل المعاني

rows.speaker: إسماعيل الضرير
rows.claim: Ismaʿil al-Darir calls the intention-to-create interpretation the correct one.
rows.anchor: وقال إسماعيل الضرير إنه الصواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti objects that this interpretation is unlikely because the word here takes ʿala; if it meant turning toward, it would take ila as in 41:11.
rows.anchor: قلت يبعده تعديته بعلى ولو كان كما ذكروه لتعدى بإلى

rows.speaker: ابن اللبان
rows.claim: Ibn al-Labban interprets God's istiwa as establishing balance through justice, giving each created thing its proper measure by wisdom.
rows.anchor: سابعها قال ابن اللبان الاستواء المنسوب إليه تعالى بمعنى اعتدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu al-Qarnayn is variously identified as Alexander, Abdullah ibn al-Dahhak ibn Saʿd, al-Mundhir ibn Maʾ al-Samaʾ, or al-Saʿb ibn Qarin ibn al-Hamal; Ibn Askar transmits two of these names.
rows.anchor: ومنها ذو القرنين واسمه إسكندر وقيل عبد الله بن الضحاك بن سعد وقيل المنذر بن ماء السماء وقيل الصعب بن قرين بن الهمال حكاهما ابن عسكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of Dhu al-Qarnayn is that he reached the two ends of the earth, east and west.
rows.anchor: ولقب ذا القرنين لأنه بلغ قرني الأرض المشرق والمغرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that he ruled Persia and Rome.
rows.anchor: وقيل لأنه ملك فارس والروم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that he had two locks or horns on his head.
rows.anchor: وقيل كان على رأسه قرنان أي ذؤابتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that he wore two horns made of gold.
rows.anchor: وقيل كان له قرنان من ذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the sides of his head were copper.
rows.anchor: وقيل كانت صفحتا رأسه من نحاس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that he had two small horns hidden by his turban.
rows.anchor: وقيل كان على رأسه قرنان صغيران تواريهما العمامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that he was struck on one horn and died, was raised, and was struck on the other.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنه ضرب على قرنه فمات ثم بعثه الله فضربوه على قرنه الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that he was noble on both sides of his family.
rows.anchor: وقيل لأنه كان كريم الطرفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that two generations of people died out during his lifetime.
rows.anchor: وقيل أنه انقرض في وقته قرنان من الناس وهو حي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that he was given knowledge of the outward and inward.
rows.anchor: وقيل لأنه أعطي علم الظاهر وعلم الباطن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that he entered the regions of light and darkness.
rows.anchor: وقيل لأنه دخل النور والظلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh is identified as al-Walid ibn Musʿab, with the kunyas Abu al-Abbas, Abu al-Walid, or Abu Murra also reported.
rows.anchor: ومنها فرعون واسمه الوليد بن مصعب وكنيته أبو العباس وقيل أبو الوليد وقيل أبو مرة

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: Some say Pharaoh was a title for every ruler of Egypt.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن فرعون لقب لكل من ملك مصر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Hatim transmits Mujahid's view that Pharaoh was Persian, from Istakhr.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن أبي حاتم عن مجاهد قال كان فرعون فارسيا من أهل إصطخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tubbaʿ is said to have been named Asʿad ibn Maliki Karib; he was called Tubbaʿ because many people followed him.
rows.anchor: ومنها تبع قيل كان اسمه أسعد بن ملكي كرب وسمى تبعا لكثرة من تبعه

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: Another view treats Tubbaʿ as a title for Yemen's kings, each following his predecessor like a caliph succeeding another.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنه لقب ملوك اليمن سمي كل واحد منهما تبعا أي يتبع صاحبه كالخليفة يخلف غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By consensus, 92:17–18 was revealed specifically about Abu Bakr; its wording is not general.
rows.anchor: فإنها نزلت في أبي بكر الصديق بالإجماع

rows.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
rows.claim: Fakhr al-Din al-Razi uses 92:17 with 49:13 to argue that Abu Bakr is the best person after the Messenger.
rows.anchor: وقد استدل بها الإمام فخر الدين الرازي مع قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that al-atqa applies generally is mistaken: the phrase has no generalizing form, since the definite article is neither relative here nor attached to a plural, and an antecedent is present.
rows.anchor: وهذا غلط فإن هذه الآية ليس فيها صيغة عموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article cannot make al-atqa relative because al cannot attach to a superlative form; al-atqa is singular, has an antecedent, and its comparative form distinguishes its referent and precludes shared participation.
rows.anchor: واللام في الأتقى ليست موصولة لأنها لا توصل بأفعل التفضيل

words: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ إِنَّا خَلَقْنَٰكُم مِّن ذَكَرٍۢ وَأُنثَىٰ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse about humanity's common origin was revealed in Mecca on the conquest day but is classified Medinan because it came after the Hijra; 5:3 is another example.
rows.anchor: مثال ما نزل بمكة وحكمه مدني

words: إن الله يأمركم أن تؤدوا الأمانات إلى أهلها
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author adds 4:58 and other verses as further examples of revelation in Mecca with Medinan classification.
rows.anchor: قلت وكذا قوله ﴿ إن الله يأمركم أن تؤدوا الأمانات إلى أهلها ﴾ في آيات أخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surat al-Mumtahana was revealed in Medina but addressed the people of Mecca, an example of Medinan revelation with a Meccan address.
rows.anchor: ومثال ما نزل بالمدينة وحكمه مكي سورة الممتحنة فإنها نزلت بالمدينة مخاطبة لأهل مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Nahl passage about those who migrated was revealed in Medina while addressing the people of Mecca.
rows.anchor: وقوله في النحل ﴿ والذين هاجروا ﴾ إلى آخرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening of Surat Baraʾa was revealed in Medina while addressing Meccan polytheists.
rows.anchor: وصدر براءة نزل بالمدينة خطابا لمشركي أهل مكة

words: الذين يجتنبون كبائر الإثم والفواحش إلا اللمم
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage on avoiding major sins resembles Medinan revelation despite appearing in a Meccan sura: major sins end in fire, fawahish incur a legal penalty, and lamam falls between them, while Mecca had no such penalties.
rows.anchor: مثال ما يشبه تنزيل المدني في السور المكية قوله في النجم

words: وإذ قالوا اللهم إن كان هذا هو الحق
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surat al-Adiyat and the cited passage in al-Anfal resemble Meccan revelation despite occurring in Medinan suras.
rows.anchor: ومثال ما يشبه تنزيل مكة في السور المدنية قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surat Yusuf and al-Ikhlas are examples of material carried from Mecca to Medina; the author adds Sabih as another example on the basis of a Bukhari report.
rows.anchor: ومثال ما حمل من مكة إلى المدينة سورة يوسف والإخلاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Examples of material carried from Medina to Mecca include the sacred-month fighting passage, the usury verse, the opening of Baraʾa, and the passage about angels taking the unjust in death.
rows.anchor: ومثال ما حمل من المدينة إلى مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text first lists 3:64 and following as material carried to Abyssinia, then says it was carried to the Romans.
rows.anchor: ومثال ما حمل إلى الحبشة ﴿ قل يا أهل الكتاب تعالوا إلى كلمة سواء ﴾ الآيات

rows.speaker: جعفر بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: The author recommends Surat Maryam as the Abyssinian example because it is authentic that Jaʿfar recited it to the Negus, as transmitted by Ahmad.
rows.anchor: وينبغي أن يمثل لما حمل إلى الحبشة بسورة مريم فقد صح أن جعفر بن أبي طالب قرأها على النجاشي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-majid means generous or noble.
rows.anchor: 1963 ﴿ المجيد ﴾ الكريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marij means mixed or confused.
rows.anchor: 1964 ﴿ مريج ﴾ مختلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Basikat palms are tall.
rows.anchor: 1965 ﴿ والنخل باسقات ﴾ طوالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fi labs means in doubt.
rows.anchor: 1966 ﴿ في لبس ﴾ شك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hab al-warid is the vein of the neck.
rows.anchor: 1967 ﴿ من حبل الوريد ﴾ الوريد عرق العنق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-masjur is explained either as contained or as kindled.
rows.anchor: 1978 ﴿ والبحر المسجور ﴾ المحبوس وقيل الموقد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tamuru means to move or shake.
rows.anchor: 1979 ﴿ يوم تمور ﴾ تحرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yudaʿʿun means they are pushed or driven forcefully.
rows.anchor: 1980 ﴿ يوم يدعون ﴾ يدفعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fakihin means delighted or pleased.
rows.anchor: 1981 ﴿ فاكهين ﴾ معجبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ma alatnahum means We did not diminish their reward.
rows.anchor: 1982 ﴿ وما ألتناهم ﴾ ما نقصناهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taʾthim means falsehood or lying.
rows.anchor: 1983 ﴿ ولا تأثيم ﴾ كذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-manun means death.
rows.anchor: 1984 ﴿ ريب المنون ﴾ المنون الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-muṣayṭirun are those who dominate and tyrannize.
rows.anchor: 1985 ﴿ المصيطرون ﴾ المسلطون الجبارون

rows.speaker: أهل البديع
rows.claim: Rhetoricians say the best rhymed cadence has equal endings, with the second clause longer as a next-best pattern and the third clause longer in a three-part series.
rows.anchor: قال أهل البديع أحسن السجع ونحوه ما تساوت قرائنه نحو

rows.speaker: ابن الأثير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Athir says the second ending should match the first or be slightly longer, and the third should be longer.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأثير الأحسن في الثانية المساواة

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: Al-Khafaji says the second ending must never be shorter than the first.
rows.anchor: وقال الخفاجي لا يجوز أن تكون الثانية أقصر من الأولى

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: Another rule favors short cadence units because they display the speaker's strength; the minimum is two words, long units exceed ten, and those between are medium, as in Surat al-Qamar.
rows.anchor: الثاني قالوا أحسن السجع ما كان قصيرا لدلالته على قوة المنشئ

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says preserving verse endings is good only when meaning and sound remain coherent; polishing sound while neglecting meaning is not eloquence.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري في كشافه القديم لا تحسن المحافظ على الفواصل لمجردها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the fronting in 2:4 is for exclusivity, not merely to fit the verse ending.
rows.anchor: وبني على ذلك أن التقديم في ﴿ وبالآخرة هم يوقنون ﴾ ليس لمجرد الفاصلة بل لرعاية الاختصاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse endings are based on pausal forms, allowing a nominative ending to match a genitive one and vice versa; the source illustrates this with several paired passages.
rows.anchor: مبنى الفواصل على الوقف ولهذا ساغ مقابلة المرفوع بالمجرور وبالعكس كقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'anic endings often use long vowels and an appended nūn to sustain melodic extension; Sībawayh notes that Arabic singers append these sounds to lengthen the voice, and the Qur'an uses easy pauses and sweet endings.
rows.anchor: كثر في القرآن ختم الفواصل بحروف المد واللين وإلحاق النون وحكمته وجود التمكن من التطريب بذلك

words: ما ضربوه لك إلا جدلا بل هم قوم خصمون
rows.speaker: رسول الله ﷺ
rows.claim: Abu Umama reports the Prophet saying that a people do not stray after guidance without being given disputation; he then recites 43:58, as transmitted by Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, and others.
rows.anchor: أخرج أحمد والترمذي وغيرهما عن أبي أمامة قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: رسول الله ﷺ
rows.claim: In a report from Abu Hurayra, every person in Hell sees his place in Paradise and regrets, saying that with God's guidance he would have been among the God-fearing.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي حاتم عن أبي هريرة قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: رسول الله ﷺ
rows.claim: The same report says each person in Paradise sees a place in Hell and gives thanks, saying that without God's guidance they would not have found the way.
rows.anchor: وكل أهل الجنة يرى منزله من النار فيقول

rows.speaker: رسول الله ﷺ
rows.claim: The report says everyone has a place in both Paradise and Hell; the unbeliever inherits the believer's place in Hell and the believer inherits the unbeliever's place in Paradise, which the source connects to 43:72.
rows.anchor: قال وقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ( ما من أحد إلا وله منزل في الجنة ومنزل في النار فالكافر يرث المؤمن

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi classifies Qur'anic revelation as celestial, terrestrial, between heaven and earth, and even beneath the earth in a cave.
rows.anchor: تقدم قول ابن العربي إن من القرآن سمائيا وأرضيا

rows.speaker: هبة الله المفسر
rows.claim: A report says revelation generally came between Mecca and Medina, except six verses said to have descended neither on earth nor in heaven: three from al-Saffat, one from al-Zukhruf, and the final two of al-Baqara on the Night Journey.
rows.anchor: أنبأنا هبة الله المفسر قال نزل القرآن بين مكة والمدينة إلا ست آيات

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi suggests the extraordinary verses meant those revealed in the space between heaven and earth; he says Surat al-Mursalat came beneath the earth in the cave, based on a sound report from Ibn Masʿud.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي ولعله أراد في الفضاء بين السماء والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti finds no support for the unusual-location claims about the earlier verses except the final al-Baqara verses; he cites Muslim's Ibn Masʿud report that at Sidrat al-Muntaha the Prophet received five prayers, the final verses of al-Baqara, and forgiveness for major sins by those avoiding shirk.
rows.anchor: قلت أما الآيات المتقدمة فلم أقف على مستند لما ذكره فيها

rows.speaker: الهذلي
rows.claim: Al-Hudhali's al-Kamil says the final verses beginning Amana al-Rasul were revealed at the distance of two bow lengths.
rows.anchor: وفي الكامل للهذلي نزلت ﴿ آمن الرسول ﴾ إلى آخرها بقاب قوسين
